note: Showcase farms for the demo. The farmers are illustrative personas, not real people. Locations were chosen and verified by Claude Code on 2026-11-14 with ESA WorldCover, USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer and NASA MODIS land cover in Google Earth Engine.

farms.name: Central Luzon rice farm
farms.persona: Illustrative smallholder rice farmer, Nueva Ecija
farms.place: Nueva Ecija province, Central Luzon, about 13 km south of the Science City of Munoz

verification.satellite_crop_pattern: MODIS NDVI 2001-2026 normal peaks in February and August (two rice crops a year) and is lowest April-June; dry-season rain is about 1 mm/day, so the dry-season crop is irrigated

farms.story: Two irrigated rice crops a year leave a hot, dry gap from April to June (35 C+ in 29-30 of the last 30 years, driest soil in April). A short, heat-tolerant legume such as mungbean could fill it. Typhoons and heavy rain are a real risk (August 2026 rain was 2.6x normal).

sources.claim: Nueva Ecija is Central Luzon's largest rice producer; PhilRice's Central Experiment Station is in the Science City of Munoz
sources.title: Daily Tribune: Central Luzon lands yield high-quality palay (2023)

sources.claim: Rice is grown in a wet season and a dry season; a cropping season lasts about 3 to 3.5 months
sources.title: DA Bureau of Plant Industry: Region III wet and dry season report, July 2018 - June 2019

sources.claim: Rice-rice-mungbean rotation: mungbean planted right after the rice harvest at the start of the dry season, valued for drought tolerance and soil fertility
sources.title: DA AMIA: Investment Prioritization for Region II, Adaptive Crop Diversification, Rotation Rice-Rice-Mungbean (2024)

sources.claim: Mungbean was the best upland crop for using residual soil moisture after rice
sources.title: AGRIS (FAO) record of a UP Los Banos study on crops after rice

sources.claim: About 20 tropical cyclones enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility each year; 8-9 cross the country
sources.title: PAGASA: Tropical Cyclone Information

farms.name: Central Iowa corn-soybean farm
farms.persona: Illustrative mechanized corn-soybean farmer, Boone County
farms.place: Rural Boone County, Iowa, west of Ames
farms.story: The classic two-crop rotation, mechanized and rain-fed. Fields sit bare from the October harvest to the May planting, through frost and snowmelt. A cereal rye cover crop could hold the soil over winter. A strong contrast with the Philippines farm.

sources.claim: This field alternated soybean and corn every year 2021-2025 (at least 99.5% of the 250 m circle in the main crop)
sources.title: USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer 2021-2025 (via Google Earth Engine, USDA/NASS/CDL)

sources.claim: Corn and soybean planting runs mid-April to early June (57% of corn and 39% of soybeans planted by May 12, 2024); harvest runs mid-September to November
sources.title: USDA NASS: Iowa Annual Crop Progress 2024

sources.claim: Cereal rye is a recommended cover crop in Iowa corn-soybean rotations, terminated before soybean planting
sources.title: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach: cover crop recipe (cereal rye)
